sections.content: Before investing, ask whether people with the problem use the channel to seek answers. sections.content: She recommends fixing the basics before paying to drive traffic: have a website, make sure it loads quickly and is discoverable, and create content if people cannot find it. answer.summary: Judge a channel by the customers and revenue it produces—not just lead volume—and weigh its economics against its audience ceiling and real user demand. Make sure the product can deliver on the promise before scaling acquisition.

sections.heading: Measure what happens after the lead
sections.content: Track the journey from lead to qualified opportunity to closed customer, then measure how much revenue customers from that channel generate one year out. Berkowitz says Deel used a real-time dashboard, including for Facebook ads, to assess payback, decide how much it could spend to win a customer, and judge whether a channel was worth investing in or had reached its investment peak. Don’t mistake high lead volume for a good channel if those leads don’t convert.

sections.heading: Check demand and the channel’s ceiling
sections.content: For cheaper channels, look for places where potential customers are already asking questions and provide useful answers. Estimate the audience’s upper limit: a subreddit of about 1,000 people, for example, is not a route to 5,000 customers; she said a more realistic possibility might be winning 10% of people there who have the problem. Likewise, writing SEO content won’t help if people aren’t searching Google for that question.

sections.heading: Check the prerequisites before scaling
sections.content: Start with a solid experience: make sure the website exists, loads quickly, and can be found before putting money behind ads; she cautions that paid ads won’t work well with a site taking more than four seconds to load. And acquisition channels won’t work if the product fails to meet expectations.

points.explanation: The answer advises tracking leads through qualified opportunities to closed customers and warns against judging a channel by lead volume when leads do not convert.
The answer says to measure revenue from channel-acquired customers one year out to assess payback, determine how much to spend to acquire a customer, and decide whether the channel merits investment.
